results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** The finite-mode conventions of the Statement. Work in grouped Schrödinger coordinates $Q=\sqrt\hbar x$, $P=-i\sqrt\hbar\partial_x$, transported by the given Fock–Schrödinger unitary when necessary. Write $p=-i\partial_x$. A normalized quadratic evolution is taken along a compact parameter interval, with a piecewise-smooth real symmetric coefficient matrix $K(t)$; the equation holds on each smooth piece on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$, with continuous matching at the joins. Its propagator and inverse preserve Schwartz space, and its trajectories are differentiable there on those pieces. No scalar or linear Hamiltonian is permitted.

[F1] The finite-mode definition supplies AC, the quadrature and Weyl conventions, the Schwartz domain and the regular irreducible Weyl system. [[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]

[F2] For a symplectic block matrix with $A$ invertible, $Y=CA^{-1}$ and $X=A^{-1}B$ are symmetric and $S=L_YD_AU_X$. Every symplectic matrix is a finite product of the elementary matrices. [[lem-nrqmx-finite-symplectic-generator-factorization]]

[F3] The Weyl system is irreducible; two unitaries inducing the same symplectic Weyl covariance differ by a scalar of modulus one. [[lem-nrqmx-finite-symplectic-implementers]]

[F4] Fourier transformation is unitary on $L^2$ and is a topological automorphism of Schwartz space. We use the unitary angular-frequency normalization $(2\pi)^{-r/2}\int e^{-ik\cdot x}f(x)\,dx$, obtained from the suppliers' frequency convention by a real dilation. [[thm-plancherel]] [[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]]



**Proof technique:** construct quadratic evolution from elementary operators near the identity, then determine its possible scalar phase from the transported Gaussian, without an imported oscillatory-kernel or Maslov-index theorem.

1.1 Put $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}$. Near the identity the block $A$ is invertible with positive determinant. For the factorization in [F2] define $C_Yf(x)=e^{ix^TYx/2}f(x)$, $E_Af(x)=(\det A)^{-1/2}f(A^{-1}x)$ and $T_X=\mathcal F^{-1}e^{-ik^TXk/2}\mathcal F$. Each is unitary by change of variables or [F4]. The product rule and linear change of variables show that each factor and its inverse act continuously on Schwartz space and depend smoothly on their parameters there. For example every derivative of a chirp is a polynomial times the same chirp, giving bounds by finitely many Schwartz seminorms, uniformly on compact parameter sets; differentiation in a parameter inserts only another polynomial or a first-order differential operator. The same argument applies in Fourier coordinates to $T_X$ by [F4]. Direct differentiation or substitution gives $C_Y^*(Q,P)^TC_Y=L_Y(Q,P)^T$, $E_A^*(Q,P)^TE_A=D_A(Q,P)^T$, and $T_X^*(Q,P)^TT_X=U_X(Q,P)^T$. The same substitutions in the explicit Weyl formula give covariance on all $L^2$. Thus $L(S):=C_YE_AT_X$ is a smooth local unitary Schwartz lift of $S$, with $L(I)=I$. [F1, F2, F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 Along a smooth local path the three logarithmic generators $i\hbar\dot C_YC_Y^{-1}$, $i\hbar\dot E_AE_A^{-1}$ and $i\hbar\dot T_XT_X^{-1}$ are respectively $-\hbar x^T\dot Yx/2$, $-i\hbar((\dot AA^{-1}x)\cdot\partial_x+\operatorname{tr}(\dot AA^{-1})/2)$ and $\hbar p^T\dot Xp/2$. The half-trace in the middle expression is exactly the symmetric ordering of the mixed position-momentum term. Product differentiation conjugates and adds these expressions. The covariance from step 1.1 replaces each quadrature by a real linear combination, so a symmetrically ordered homogeneous quadratic stays exactly such a quadratic, with no extra scalar. If its coefficient matrix is $K_L$, differentiating the covariance and using $[R_j,R_k]=i\hbar(J_0)_{jk}$ gives $\dot S=J_0K_LS$, hence $K_L=-J_0\dot SS^{-1}$. Equality of the quadratic coefficients is literal: the coefficients of second derivatives, of $x_j\partial_k$, and of $x_jx_k$ determine the three real blocks, including the symmetric-order half-trace. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Given any piecewise-smooth symmetric $K(t)$, let $S(0)=I$ solve the finite matrix equation $\dot S=J_0K(t)S$. Its solution exists throughout the compact interval by the usual integral series: on a piece where $\|J_0K\|\le C$, the $n$th iterated integral is bounded by $C^nt^n/n!$; the series and its derivative converge uniformly. Differentiating $S^TJ_0S$ gives zero, so $S$ stays symplectic. A finite subdivision makes every $S(t)S(t_j)^{-1}$ lie in the local neighborhood of step 1.1 on its subinterval. Define $U(0)=I$ and $U(t)=L(S(t)S(t_j)^{-1})U(t_j)$ there. Step 2.1 gives exactly $i\hbar\dot U=H_KU$, where $H_K=\tfrac14\sum_{a,b}K_{ab}(R_aR_b+R_bR_a)$; these are unitary Schwartz automorphisms, continuous at the joins. The expression is symmetric on Schwartz space by integration by parts. Two Schwartz solutions of the same equation with the same initial vector agree, because the derivative of their squared $L^2$ difference is zero. This proves uniqueness first on Schwartz space and then, by density and unitarity, on $L^2$. The constructed propagator has covariance $U(t)^*W(z)U(t)=W(S(t)^Tz)$ by the finite product covariance; every normalized propagator agrees with this one by uniqueness. This also proves existence and covariance rather than assuming a time-slicing limit. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Write $K=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b^T&d\end{pmatrix}$ with $a,d$ real symmetric, and $S=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}$. Set $F=A+iB$ and $G=C+iD$. The symplectic block relations give $F^*G-G^*F=2iI$ and $F^TG=G^TF$. If $Fv=0$, multiplying the first identity by $v^*$ and $v$ forces $\|v\|^2=0$; thus $F$ is invertible at every time, even at a singular generating chart. Consequently $Z:=GF^{-1}$ is symmetric and $\operatorname{Im}Z=(Z-Z^*)/(2i)=F^{-*}F^{-1}>0$. The classical equation gives $\dot F=(b^T+dZ)F$ and $\dot Z=-a-bZ-Zb^T-ZdZ$, with $F(0)=I$ and $Z(0)=iI$. [F1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Let $c(0)=1$ and $\dot c/c=-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(b+dZ)$, defining $c$ by the exponential of the integral of this continuous, piecewise-smooth coefficient. It never vanishes. Define $g(t,x)=\pi^{-r/4}c(t)\exp(ix^TZ(t)x/2)$. Positive definiteness of $\operatorname{Im}Z$ makes $g$ Schwartz, smoothly in time on each piece; compact time sets have a uniform positive lower eigenvalue, so all required Schwartz and $L^2$ differentiations are justified by polynomial times Gaussian bounds. In these dimensionless coordinates $H_K/\hbar=\tfrac12(x^Tax+x^Tbp+p^Tb^Tx+p^Tdp)$. Applying this differential expression to $g$ gives $H_Kg/\hbar=\bigl(x^T(a+bZ+Zb^T+ZdZ)x/2-i\operatorname{tr}(b+dZ)/2\bigr)g$. Steps 4.1 and the equation for $c$ identify this with $i\partial_tg$. As $g(0)=g_0:=\pi^{-r/4}e^{-|x|^2/2}$, the uniqueness in step 3.1 gives $U(t)g_0=g(t)$. No physical-coordinate factor of $\hbar$ is missing: both the Schrödinger equation and the quadratic contain that common factor. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Differentiating the determinant by its finite polynomial formula gives $(\det F)'=(\det F)\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}\dot F)$. Since the trace of $b^T$ equals the trace of $b$, steps 4.1 and 5.1 give $(c^2\det F)'=0$. The initial value is one, hence $c(t)^2\det(A(t)+iB(t))=1$. This identity holds through all subdivision joins by continuity. It uses neither a choice of a global square root nor a real generating-chart denominator. [step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 For the two endpoint propagators of the Statement, step 3.1 supplies the same Weyl covariance at their common $S$. By [F3], $U_2=\lambda U_1$ with $|\lambda|=1$. Step 4.1 gives the same endpoint $Z$ for both Gaussian vectors, and step 6.1 gives $c_2^2=c_1^2=1/\det(A+iB)$. Since $c_1\ne0$, $\lambda=c_2/c_1$ and $\lambda^2=1$, so $U_2=\pm U_1$. This proves the required invertible-$B$ claim and in fact the same phase conclusion at every endpoint. Multiplying both unitaries by any fixed normalized quadratic propagator preserves their relative sign, proving the final clause. [F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎



The historical title records the phase-parity application. The proof establishes the stated sign ambiguity by an ordinary finite Gaussian differential equation; it imports no Maslov-index, path-integral convergence, or metaplectic-cover theorem. The cited literature remains attribution for the established statement. No new full-text source reading or external proof acceptance is asserted by this local reconstruction.

**Given:** AC, $r\ge1$, $\hbar>0$, the finite-mode quadrature and Weyl
conventions of [[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]], and
$S^TJS=J$.

[A1] AC is the explicit choice hypothesis of the finite-dimensional
Stone–von Neumann theorem and supplies Countable Choice where needed
([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[A2] The matrix $S$ is real symplectic, $r\ge1$, and $\hbar>0$ under the
quadrature and Weyl conventions in the Statement.

[F1] The local Weyl system has the stated fixed central parameter, regularity,
and irreducibility. Every nonzero irreducible regular finite-dimensional Weyl
system with this same nonzero parameter is unitarily equivalent to it
([[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]],
[[thm-stone-von-neumann-for-finite-dimensional-weyl-systems]],
[[thm-nrqmx-finite-weyl-uniqueness-interface]]).

[F2] Every finite symplectic matrix factors into symmetric shears, invertible
coordinate changes, and partial Fourier rotations, including when its initial
upper-left block is singular
([[lem-nrqmx-finite-symplectic-generator-factorization]]).

[F3] Every such symplectic matrix has a unitary Weyl implementer, and two
implementers of the same Weyl automorphism differ only by phase
([[lem-nrqmx-finite-symplectic-implementers]]).

[F4] The local reconstruction in the Proof of [[lem-nrqmx-finite-maslov-phase-parity]], steps 1.1–1.3, constructs the unique normalized propagator for every piecewise-smooth real homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonian. It is a unitary Schwartz automorphism, depends continuously on time together with its inverse, and has the Weyl covariance of its classical matrix solution. Near the identity a smooth local lift is $L(S)=C_{CA^{-1}}E_AT_{A^{-1}B}$, with the chirp, coordinate and Fourier-multiplier factors explicitly defined there. Their parameter derivatives are homogeneous symmetrically ordered quadratics, and their Schwartz seminorm bounds are locally uniform. This is a proved local construction, not an external time-slicing theorem.

[F5] The same supplier proves the sign ambiguity for normalized quadratic propagators with the same endpoint. Its Proof, steps 2.1–2.3, obtains $Z=(C+iD)(A+iB)^{-1}$ and $c^2\det(A+iB)=1$ for the transported vacuum; step 2.3 combines this with phase uniqueness to give $U_2=\pm U_1$. In particular its stated generating-chart conclusion is available, and the local calculation actually applies at all endpoints. [[lem-nrqmx-finite-maslov-phase-parity]]

[F6] The one-mode oscillator has normalized eigenvectors $|n\rangle$ with
$H=\frac12(Q^2+P^2)=\hbar(N+\frac12)$ and $N|n\rangle=n|n\rangle$
([[lem-nrqmx-finite-mode-fock-schr-identification]],
[[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]]).



1.1 Reorder interleaved coordinates by the fixed permutation $P(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)$, and write $W_g(w)=W(P^Tw)$ for grouped labels. Then $J_0=PJP^T$ and $S_g=PSP^T$ obeys $S_g^TJ_0S_g=J_0$. Apply [F3] directly to the grouped Weyl system on $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ with label matrix $S_g^T$; this matrix is symplectic because $S_g^TJ_0S_g=J_0$ also implies $S_gJ_0S_g^T=J_0$. Since $S_g^TP=PS^T$, converting labels back gives $$M_S^*W(z)M_S=M_S^*W_g(Pz)M_S=W_g(S_g^TPz)=W(S^Tz).$$ Differentiating the bounded one-parameter Weyl identity on the common Schwartz core gives $M_S^*RM_S=SR$. For the rest of the proof use grouped coordinates and write $S$ for $S_g$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Define $\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ as the set of endpoints of the normalized evolutions in [F4] along piecewise-smooth coefficient paths $K(t)=K(t)^T$, with $H_t=\tfrac14\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}(t)(R_jR_k+R_kR_j)$ and no linear or scalar term. The operator acts on the common Schwartz space. Concatenation gives products: first evolve by $U_2$, then evolve by $U_1$ with its initial vector $U_2f$, obtaining $U_1U_2$. The reversed evolution $U(T-t)U(T)^{-1}$ starts at $I$, ends at $U(T)^{-1}$, and is generated by $-H_{T-t}$, so inverses also belong to the set. By [F4], each endpoint implements the symplectic solution $\dot S=J_0K(t)S$. If two matrices had the same implementing unitary, differentiating their Weyl covariances on Schwartz space would give $(S-S')R=0$. Applied to the vacuum, $Q_kg_0=\sqrt{\hbar/2}g_{e_k}$ and $P_kg_0=i\sqrt{\hbar/2}g_{e_k}$ by [F6]; the reality of the rows forces both their position and momentum coefficients to vanish. Thus the endpoint is unique. For two lifts, $\pi(M_1M_2)=\pi(M_1)\pi(M_2)$ by conjugating the quadratures, so $\pi$ is a homomorphism. [F1, F4, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 Every generator from [F2] is a path endpoint of a homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonian. A symmetric shear is joined to the identity by scaling its symmetric block, and a partial Fourier rotation is joined by varying the oscillator angle. If $\det A>0$, polar decomposition writes $A=OP$ with $O\in SO(r)$ and $P$ positive definite. The path $P_t=(1-t)I+tP$ stays positive definite, and an orthogonal matrix in $SO(r)$ is a product of plane rotations, each joined to the identity by varying its angle. These paths connect the coordinate change to the identity. If $\det A<0$, factor one coordinate reflection from a positive-determinant change; that reflection is a $\pi$ oscillator rotation on that mode. This gives a piecewise-smooth symplectic path for each generator. Along any such path $S_t$, the matrix $X_t=\dot S_tS_t^{-1}$ satisfies $X_t^TJ_0+J_0X_t=0$; hence $K_t=-J_0X_t$ is symmetric and $\dot S_t=J_0K_tS_t$. The symmetrically ordered quadratic with matrix $K_t$ therefore has this classical endpoint. Thus [F2] supplies, for every $S$, a product of normalized quadratic propagators whose endpoint is $S$, proving $\pi$ is onto. The one-parameter paths also show that each such product belongs to the identity component of $\operatorname{Mp}$. [F2, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 If $M_1,M_2$ implement the same $S$, then [F3] makes $M_2M_1^*=\lambda I$ for some $|\lambda|=1$. For any other representation $W'$ in [F1], choose a unitary $V$ with $VW'(z)V^*=W(z)$ by the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem. Then $M'_S=V^*M_SV$ is unitary and $$M_S'^*W'(z)M'_S=V^*M_S^*W(z)M_SV=W'(S^Tz).$$ Conjugating the phase-uniqueness statement by $V$ proves the same result in that representation. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 If two normalized lifts lie over the same grouped matrix $S$, the Gaussian determinant calculation in [F5] makes them differ by sign. This already holds for every $S$: the matrix $A+iB$ used there is invertible by symplecticity, including when either real block is singular. In particular it supplies the required invertible-$B$ chart argument without an imported Maslov-index parity formula. Thus every fiber has at most two elements. [F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The identity has two distinct lifts. The constant zero Hamiltonian gives $I$. On the first mode (and as the identity on the other modes if $r>1$), the homogeneous oscillator path $U(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}=e^{-it(N+1/2)}$ has classical endpoint the identity at $t=2\pi$, because its Hamilton equations are $\dot Q=P$, $\dot P=-Q$ and make one full rotation, while by [F6] $$U(2\pi)|n\rangle=e^{-2\pi i(n+1/2)}|n\rangle=-|n\rangle$$ for every $n$. Completeness of the Hermite basis gives $U(2\pi)=-I$. For any $S$, choose a normalized lift $\widetilde M_S$ supplied by step 2.1. Then $\widetilde M_S$ and $-\widetilde M_S$ are two distinct lifts; step 2.3 proves there are no others. The kernel is exactly $\{I,-I\}$. [F4, F6, step 2.1, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 Fix $S_0$ and a normalized lift $M_0$. On a matrix neighborhood $\mathcal B$ of $S_0$ small enough that $SS_0^{-1}$ lies in the local neighborhood of [F4], put $\sigma(S)=L(SS_0^{-1})M_0$. The local factors are endpoints of homogeneous quadratic paths starting at the identity, as proved in [F4], so $\sigma(S)$ belongs to $\operatorname{Mp}$ and has endpoint $S$. It depends continuously on $S$, as does its inverse, pointwise in the Schwartz topology: the explicit chirp and linear-coordinate factors have uniformly bounded seminorm estimates on compact parameter neighborhoods, and the Fourier factors are fixed continuous maps. These estimates also justify continuity when composing such a varying local factor with a varying Schwartz vector. Step 3.1 shows every lift over $S$ is exactly $\sigma(S)$ or $-\sigma(S)$. [F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 The endpoint map is continuous for the specified operator topology, without assuming joint continuity of arbitrary Schwartz-operator composition. For each row $j$ and mode $k$, covariance and [F6] give $\langle R_jMg_0,Mg_{e_k}\rangle=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(S_{j,Q_k}+iS_{j,P_k})$, where the pairing is linear in its first argument. On the left $R_j$ is continuous on Schwartz space, its inclusion into $L^2$ is continuous, and only the two fixed input vectors $g_0,g_{e_k}$ are used. Thus every real matrix entry of $\pi(M)$ is continuous. Over $\mathcal B$, the scalar $\varepsilon(M):=\langle Mg_0,\sigma(\pi(M))g_0\rangle$ is continuous, takes exactly the values $+1,-1$, and distinguishes the two lifts since $\|g_0\|=1$. Therefore the two inverse images $\varepsilon^{-1}(1)$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}(-1)$ in $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal B)$ are disjoint open sheets; on each, $\pi$ and $\pm\sigma$ are continuous inverse maps onto $\mathcal B$. This proves the two-fold covering in the given topology. [F4, F6, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The same charts make the set a topological group. Locally its elements are $\varepsilon\sigma(S)$. Products and inverses of their explicit finite-parameter factors depend continuously on the matrix parameters and on each Schwartz vector, by the uniform seminorm bounds in step 4.1; their endpoint matrices multiply and invert continuously. The sign relative to a local section at the resulting endpoint is recovered by the continuous vacuum pairing in step 5.1. Hence multiplication and inversion are continuous in these charts, which have precisely the operator topology by step 5.1. Finally every defining normalized path is continuous in that topology by [F4], including its inverse path, so it joins its endpoint to $I$. Consequently the group is path connected. Together with step 3.1 this proves the connected double cover with kernel $\{I,-I\}$ and its defining unitary action, retaining the unrestricted phase ambiguity only for arbitrary individual Weyl implementers. [F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎
